items.prompt: What is relationship capital?
choices: Goodwill built from earlier small, genuine help
A formal title that lets you give orders to people
A written list of favors other people owe you
items.explanation: It is trust earned through earlier help, not authority and not a ledger.

items.prompt: Which act is a genuine deposit?
choices: Doing a big favor the day before you need one
Answering a coworker's quick question when they ask
Telling the boss how much you have helped others
items.explanation: Small, low-cost help with no visible follow-up ask reads as genuine.

items.prompt: What is the test for a genuine deposit?
choices: Did the other person say thank you right away?
Was the favor large enough to be remembered?
Would it still make sense if nothing were asked back?
items.explanation: If you would help anyway, it is a deposit rather than a setup.

items.prompt: Why are small deposits better than one large gesture?
choices: They cost little and carry no visible ask
They are less likely to be noticed by anyone at all
They let you keep a precise count of what is owed
items.explanation: A pattern of small help reads as character; one big favor reads as an event.

items.prompt: What is the favor economy?
choices: The official budget a company sets aside for gifts
The informal system of help that follows relationship history
A paid service where employees trade tasks for money
items.explanation: It runs on trust built between people, not on job titles or contracts.

items.prompt: A classmate shared notes with you all term. You forget your book. Who is more likely to help you?
choices: A stranger, since they owe you nothing at all
Nobody, because favors never carry over to later
The classmate, because trust already exists
items.explanation: Earlier help is why the classmate says yes quickly.

items.prompt: What does banking goodwill mean?
choices: Offering small help before you need anything back
Saving up favors so you can cash them all at once
Asking for help early so you build a long history
items.explanation: The deposit comes first and asks nothing in return.

items.prompt: Which timing makes a favor look like a ploy?
choices: A quick answer given months before any request
A big favor right before a known request
A short review done because you were asked once
items.explanation: Proximity to the ask reveals the purpose.

items.prompt: Which of these three acts is most clearly a genuine deposit?
choices: Sending a large gift to the person who approves your budget next week
Sharing a template you made, with no request pending from anyone
Offering to cover a shift right after learning they decide your bonus
Praising a colleague loudly before asking them for a favor
items.explanation: Only the first would still make sense if nothing were ever asked. The other three are timed to a decision or an ask.
items.reference:
Deposit or ploy?
✅ deposit: help you would give anyone, asked nothing back
⚠️ ploy: big favor timed next to a known request
🔎 test: would it still make sense if nothing came back?
Why: the same act can build or burn trust, depending on whether it reads as free.
items.learnMore:
Genuine deposits

Relationship capital comes from small, low-cost help that carries no visible follow-up ask. Size and timing decide how it reads.

Common mistake

Believing a bigger favor builds more capital. A large favor right before an ask reads as a setup.
items.reflection: Think of someone who helped you with no strings. What about how they did it made it feel genuine?

items.prompt: You review a colleague's change unprompted. You also know they will approve your budget next quarter. Is the review a ploy?
choices: Yes, because any later overlap between you disqualifies the help
Yes, unless you promise to ask for nothing over the next year
No, if you would have reviewed it regardless of who they were
No, but only after you tell them about the upcoming budget
items.explanation: The test is intent and proximity, not whether any future connection exists. Nearly every working relationship has some.

Both equally, since each of them helped someone who lives nearby
Neither, because help only counts when it is repaid in kind
Rafa's, because repeated small acts with no ask form a pattern
items.explanation: A pattern of small acts reads as character, while one favor next to an ask reads as a trade.

choices: A hidden tally shapes behavior and tends to show eventually
The tally is too small to affect anything that happens later
Mental tallies are harmless as long as nobody hears them
The flaw is only that they said the tally out loud to you
items.explanation: Expecting a return changes how and when you help, and receivers pick that up even when it is unspoken.

items.prompt: What is transactional keeping-score?
choices: Writing thank-you notes after each favor you receive
Treating each favor as a debt to be tracked and collected
Remembering who helped you so you can help them back
items.explanation: The tracking itself is what changes how the help is received.

items.prompt: Why does a visible tally backfire?
choices: People forget how many favors they have really done
It makes the favors themselves harder to give at all
People feel tracked and become guarded instead of generous
items.explanation: Help builds trust only while it looks free.

items.prompt: What does 'quid pro quo' mean?
choices: This for that
Many hands make light work
As soon as possible
items.explanation: It names an exchange in which each side gives only because of what it receives.

items.prompt: Which message treats past help as a debt?
choices: I am stuck, could you spare five minutes?
I helped you four times, so you owe me
Thanks again for the help last month
items.explanation: Citing favors as leverage recasts them as prepayments.

items.prompt: Reciprocity norms are best described as...
choices: A written rule that every favor must be repaid
A tax people pay once a year at work
A shared feeling that kindness deserves kindness
items.explanation: They are social feelings, not entries in a ledger.

items.prompt: Which situation hurts trust most?
choices: Doing a favor and asking for one right after
Doing a favor and never mentioning it again
Doing a favor and being thanked by the person
items.explanation: The nearby ask makes the favor look bought.

items.prompt: Is every exchange of favors bad?
choices: Yes, any exchange ruins the relationship
No, openly agreed trades are honest
Yes, but only when the amounts are unequal
items.explanation: The problem is disguising a trade as free help.

items.prompt: What is a healthier habit than tracking?
choices: Writing down each favor for later review
Asking people to promise to help back soon
Helping when it is easy and letting it go
items.explanation: Letting go keeps the help looking, and being, free.

items.prompt: Maya reminds a classmate she shared notes four times before asking for theirs. The history is real. What is the likely effect?
choices: The classmate learns something new and weighs her request more
Nothing changes, since the history was real in every detail
The classmate feels more trust because Maya is being honest
The earlier help starts to look like a prepayment she is collecting
items.explanation: The classmate remembers the notes already, so the reminder adds no persuasion. It only reveals that Maya was counting.
items.reference:
Gift or invoice?
🎁 free: no tally, no nearby ask, no reminder
🧾 trade: tally, reminder, or ask right after the favor
🤝 open trade: agreed in advance, so it is honest
Why: a favor that looks like a prepayment makes the receiver guarded instead of generous.
items.learnMore:
Why a tally backfires

Reciprocity norms are a shared feeling, not a ledger. Making the tally visible turns goodwill into a bill.

Common mistake

Thinking the problem is trading itself. Openly agreed trades are honest; disguised ones are not.
items.reflection: When has someone reminding you of a past favor made you less willing to help, even though the favor was real?

items.prompt: Sam helps a teammate on Monday and asks them for a favor on Tuesday. Why might it still read as a trade even if Sam meant the help sincerely?
choices: The one-day gap makes the help look bought after the fact
Tuesday is too late for any earlier help to still count
Sincerity is invisible, so only the size of the favor matters
The teammate cannot reliably remember a favor from yesterday
items.explanation: Proximity signals quid pro quo regardless of intent. Time and distance help help read as goodwill.

items.prompt: What is a cold ask?
choices: A request sent late at night when others are away
A request made in a harsh or unfriendly tone
A request to someone who has no history with you
items.explanation: It means no earlier relationship to lean on.

items.prompt: What is standing?
choices: How much trust you already have with someone
Your position on the company chart in a meeting
How long you can stay in one place at a time
items.explanation: Standing is the credit you start a request with.

items.prompt: Which cold ask is easiest to grant?
choices: A broad request to review the whole project soon
One small, specific need with a stated cost
A vague hint that you could use some help
items.explanation: Specific, bounded asks show what a yes would cost.

items.prompt: Which phrase makes a no easier to give?
choices: I am sure you will be glad to help
I already told my boss you said yes
No worries if tonight is not possible
items.explanation: A graceful exit lowers pressure on the other person.

items.prompt: Should a cold ask pretend a friendship exists?
choices: No, it is discovered quickly and costs credibility
Yes, it makes the person feel more comfortable
Yes, but only when the deadline is very close
items.explanation: Honesty is cheaper than a stretched story.

items.prompt: Is a cold ask doomed?
choices: Yes, strangers never help anyone at work
No, but it starts from zero standing
No, it is guaranteed to work if worded well
items.explanation: Good wording helps, but it does not create history.

items.prompt: Why state how long the favor will take?
choices: So you can hide how large the favor truly is
So you can hold them to an exact amount of time
So the other person can see the cost of saying yes
items.explanation: A visible, small cost makes yes easier.

items.prompt: Why mention why it is urgent?
choices: It gives a short, true reason the ask matters now
It lets you skip describing what you actually need
It makes the other person feel guilty if they refuse
items.explanation: A brief true reason helps the receiver judge.

items.prompt: Jon needs notes tonight and has never spoken to the classmate. Which message is the best cold ask?
choices: Hey buddy, you know how much we have helped each other, so send everything tonight.
Could I photograph pages 4 to 6 of your notes tonight? Five minutes, and no worries if not.
Please send me your notes, I need them urgently and would be very grateful.
I heard you are friendly, so I assume it is fine to ask for all your notes.
items.explanation: The first names a small need, states the cost, and gives an easy no. The others fabricate history or stay vague.
items.reference:
Warm ask vs. cold ask
🔥 warm: history exists, ask can be brief
❄️ cold: no history, the ask itself must be easy
📝 shape: smallest need, stated cost, easy no
Why: a cold ask cannot borrow trust it has not earned, so it has to be small and clear.
items.learnMore:
Making a cold ask

With no standing, the request carries all the weight. Specific, bounded, and truthful asks are easiest to grant.

Common mistake

Pretending a relationship exists. It is discovered quickly and costs more than asking plainly.
items.reflection: Recall asking a stranger for help. What about how they asked made it easy or hard to say yes?

items.prompt: A well-worded cold ask goes to a busy team. What is the realistic outcome?
choices: It is certain to be prioritized because it is worded so well
It will be rejected outright, since strangers never get any help at work from a busy team
It may still be queued behind requests from people the team already knows
It will be answered first because it states a clear deadline
items.explanation: Wording lowers the cost of yes, but standing decides much of the order.

It makes the request longer than it needs to be

It is quickly checked against what the other person remembers
items.explanation: A stretched story damages credibility far more than asking plainly.

choices: A first message to a team you have never worked with
A request to a friend who owes you a favor from last month
A follow-up to a coworker you chat with every day
A request to a manager who knows your work well
items.explanation: Cold means no earlier relationship, regardless of how urgent or polite the message is.

items.prompt: Priya has no standing with finance. What honest option does she have?
choices: Say she has worked with finance many times before
Ask someone who has standing to introduce her request
Wait until finance forgets she has not worked with them
items.explanation: Honest borrowing names who has the history.

items.prompt: Whose capital pays when Wren vouches for Priya?
choices: Priya's
Finance's
Wren's
items.explanation: Priya has none of her own, so the credit comes from Wren.

items.prompt: What should an honest introduction say?
choices: Who knows the team and that this request is real
That Priya and finance are already close friends
That finance is required to say yes this time
items.explanation: It says who has the history and who does not.

items.prompt: Is vouching free for the person who does it?
choices: Yes, because trust is never limited in any way
No, it uses a bit of their own reserve
Yes, as long as the request is small enough
items.explanation: A vouch spends credibility, so it should be honest and occasional.

items.prompt: How does a reserve of goodwill grow back?
choices: By asking the same favor again and again
By waiting without doing anything for a while
Through further small, genuine help
items.explanation: New deposits replenish what introductions spend.

items.prompt: In the teaching model, which gives more modeled willingness?
choices: Four deposits, at about 55%
Three deposits, at about 45%
Zero deposits, at about 18%
items.explanation: The model gives 0, 18, 33, 45, 55 for 0 through 4 deposits.

items.prompt: In the model, which deposits add the most?
choices: The last few
The first few
All of them equally
items.explanation: Willingness rises fast at first, then levels off.

items.prompt: Why should capital be spent carefully?
choices: It disappears completely after a single use
It cannot be spent without breaking the law
It is finite and grows back only through new help
items.explanation: Spending is fine, but it lowers the margin for the next ask.

items.prompt: Priya asks Wren to introduce her request. Which version keeps both of them credible?
choices: Wren says Priya and finance have always worked together closely
Wren says finance must prioritize this one for her sake
Wren says nothing, and Priya simply drops Wren's name
Wren says Priya is new to finance but the request is real
items.explanation: The honest version names the history gap and lends real standing. The others claim or hide something.
items.reference:
Lending standing
🧑 Wren: has earned standing with finance
🙋 Priya: has none, so she asks Wren to vouch
📉 cost: the vouch draws down Wren's reserve
Why: an honest introduction lends real credibility, and the lender's reserve is smaller afterwards.
items.learnMore:
Borrowing credibility honestly

An introduction spends the introducer's capital. It stays honest by saying who has history and who does not.

Common mistake

Treating a vouch as free. Repeated vouching without new deposits uses up the lender's standing.
items.reflection: When has someone vouched for you? What did it cost them, and how could you repay it with new help?

Priya's own standing with finance drops to zero overnight
There is no risk, since trust is unlimited between coworkers who generally like each other
items.explanation: Repeated vouching without replenishing draws down the lender's reserve until the word moves nothing.
